or_northeast_oregon.blurb: A quiet corner of the state centred on La Grande, where a small but committed group of climbers has been developing crags for about thirty years. Sport leads, trad comes second, and there is a little alpine climbing in the Wallowa Mountains. Grades run from easy fifth class to 5.13, most often 5.10. Spring Mountain, in the Blue Mountains at about 4,600 feet, is a wall of mostly solid andesite about 100 feet tall, with face climbing on ledges, crimps and roofs, best from late spring through early fall. Burnt River Canyon is arid, with scattered buttresses of marble that climbers call limestone, mostly bolted, good in autumn through spring, and shady or sunny depending on which crag you pick.

ut_glen_canyon.blurb: A high-desert region of south-central Utah in the Glen Canyon National Recreation Area, around Lake Powell. Most of what is climbed here is bouldering, centred on Big Water at about 4,000 feet, where sandstone blocks have tumbled down from the Straight Cliff onto gray shale, giving a moonlike look. Much of the rock is loose, so choose dark varnished stone and avoid pale, powdery faces. Problems are mostly slabby, on crimps, pockets and compression, with few overhangs, and grades run from V0 to V7, mostly V1 to V3. Lake Powell holds most of the trad lines. Early spring, late fall and winter are best; summer is very hot, with biting gnats in early summer.

ca_black_mountain.blurb: A premier bouldering zone in the San Jacinto Mountains of Southern California, at roughly 7,000 to 7,500 feet in the San Bernardino National Forest. Hundreds of granite boulders lie among pine forest, talus and ridges, and the zones are spread out. Almost all of the climbing is bouldering, from V0 to V12, with the bulk in the V0 to V5 range. Boulder Basin is the largest area and has tall, imposing problems, followed by Groupsites, The Summit and OK Corral. The granite is grippy but sharp on skin, and grades have a reputation for being stiff. Spring and fall are best; summer works in early mornings and shade, and winter is often snowed in.

ca_mammoth_lakes_bouldering.blurb: A collection of bouldering areas in and around the town of Mammoth Lakes in the Eastern Sierra, at about 7,000 feet, with spectacular views. All of it is bouldering, weighted heavily to the easy end, with a large share at V0 or below and a thin top end reaching V11. Way Lake is the biggest zone, followed by The Ravine, the Geophysics Wall and the Knowledge Boulders. Some areas can be climbed all year, while others need a hike and are reachable only in summer. It is handy for anyone staying in town, though the zones are scattered rather than concentrated in one place.

qc_03_portneuf.blurb: A climbing region between Quebec City and Mauricie, made up of Lac Long, the Vallée du Bras-du-Nord and St-Alban. Lac Long is the largest part, with cliffs on either side of a lake and the stream that drains it, and an ethic that favours traditional protection over bolts where gear fits. Trad is the biggest share overall, followed by sport, with a good number of winter mixed and ice routes and a few boulder problems. Summer grades run from 5.6 to 5.13, concentrated at 5.10 and 5.11, while ice climbs are mostly WI4 to WI5 and mixed lines M6 to M8. Multi-pitch lines are common, up to several pitches long.

ca_suicide_rock_2.blurb: The smaller of the two granite domes above Idyllwild in the San Jacinto Mountains of Riverside County, California. The granite is solid and fine-grained, polished very smooth in places such as the Weeping Wall, and rougher and more featured elsewhere. Traditional climbing dominates, with routes mostly one to three pitches, covering slabs, faces and plenty of cracks. Sport lines exist but are the exception, and even bolted routes can be runout. Grades run from easy fifth class to 5.13, most in the 5.10 to 5.11 range. Other sections include the Buttress of Cracks, Eagle Pinnacle and the North Face.
